How Tides Work

By Ada Ocean

Tides are caused mostly by the gravitational pull of the moon, which tugs on the oceans and raises a bulge of water on the side of the Earth facing it. A second bulge forms on the far side, because the Earth itself is pulled toward the moon slightly more than the distant water is.

As the Earth rotates through these two bulges, most coastlines see two high tides and two low tides every lunar day, which lasts about twenty-four hours and fifty minutes. Read more about the author, or share this.

The sun matters too. When the sun, moon, and Earth line up, at new moon and full moon, their pulls combine into larger spring tides. When they sit at right angles, at the quarter moons, the pulls partly cancel and we get smaller neap tides.

Local geography shapes all of this. Funnel-shaped bays, like the Bay of Fundy, amplify the incoming water into some of the largest tidal ranges on the planet, while enclosed seas, such as the Mediterranean, barely notice the tides at all.
